timeline.description: Chemist Georg Eppenstein rises to managing director of Ruilos, maker of garlic-based remedies and hygiene products in Köpenick.
timeline.longDescription: A group of Breslau merchants founded the publicly traded company Ruilos-Hausmittel-Heilverfahren-Volksgesellschaft m.b.H. on April 6, 1921, to manufacture and sell chemical products for medicinal and home hygiene purposes – from pharmaceutical remedies to disinfectants and preservatives, advertised with the motto 'The sun is the best medicine'. Renamed Ruilos Knoblauch-Verwertungs-G.m.b.H., the business was transferred to Berlin in 1923 and, at the height of the inflation crisis, relocated to Achenbach Strasse in Köpenick. It recovered and raised its capital stock from 6,000 to 58,000 Reich marks with additional shareholders in 1925 – one of them doctor of chemistry Georg Eppenstein, who applied his knowledge to develop patents for 'garlic therapy'. Appointed deputy manager in 1927, then managing director, he increased his holding to 52,000 Reich marks by 1930 and in 1931 moved with his family to an apartment on the production site at Achenbach Strasse 33-35. His wife Marta became deputy manager.

timeline.description: During the 'Köpenick week of blood', SA men abduct and torture Georg Eppenstein. He dies of his injuries on August 3, 1933.
timeline.longDescription: Köpenick's 'week of blood' formed a climax of the SA's early terrorist practice. From the morning of June 21, 1933, SA stormtroop unit 15 led by Herbert Gehrke began arresting political opponents and Jews; over the following days SA men abducted and tortured over 130 people, and at least 23 died. One of those abducted was Georg Eppenstein. His wife Marta secured his release from the Köpenick local court jail: 'I was shocked when I saw him. He was unrecognizable. His spectacles were gone, his eyes and head beaten in, his nose shattered. His whole face was black. My husband could not see or hear.' Diagnosed with an intradural hematoma, he underwent an operation on August 2, 1933, but succumbed to his severe brain hemorrhaging a day later, aged 65.

timeline.description: Marta and Elisabeth-Charlotte Eppenstein carry on the business; declared 'Aryan' in 1938, they save their livelihood – and their lives.
timeline.longDescription: Marta and Elisabeth-Charlotte Eppenstein took over the shareholdings and management of the company. Fearing further attacks, they moved away from Köpenick in 1934, first to Tiergarten, then in 1935 to Schlüter Strasse 49 in Charlottenburg, which became the company's base; the factory remained in Köpenick. In 1938, just weeks before the November pogrom, Marta Eppenstein declared her non-Jewish status as an 'Aryan', probably saving her and her daughter's livelihood and lives. As a 'first-degree half-Jew', Elisabeth-Charlotte had been unable to complete her study of medicine; from February to April 1944 she was interned in the Wittenauer Heilanstalten mental home.

timeline.description: The divided city forces Ruilos into liquidation; the SA perpetrators are tried in 1950. A commemorative brass stone was laid in 2004.
timeline.longDescription:
After the war, the Eppensteins were once again caught in the machinery of political systems: the production plant lay in East Berlin, the offices in the west, and the two could not be coordinated. In summer 1950 East Berlin's municipal council closed the production site, and the company went into liquidation from December 31, 1951. In 1950 the East Berlin district court tried the SA perpetrators of the 'Köpenick Blood Week' – Marta Eppenstein made a statement before the trial began, and her husband's portrait hung in the courtroom. The court sentenced 15 of the accused to death, including Gustav Erpel, executed on February 20, 1951. Marta Eppenstein was recognized as an 'approved victim of Fascism' in 1946; she died in 1957, nearly 80. Her daughter Elisabeth-Charlotte, who fought in the 1950s for recognition as a victim of political and racist persecution, died in 1973.

The site today

In 1971 the factory and family residence were demolished to make way for new development. At the former company base at Achenbach Strasse 33-35 (today Salvador Allende Strasse 43-45) in Köpenick, a commemorative brass stone for Dr. Georg Eppenstein was laid in 2004. A memorial site commemorating the 'Köpenick week of blood' opened in the former district court jail on May 8, 1980.
